title: Messaging & Event-Driven Systems Handbook
summary: Quick revision notes on queues vs pub/sub, Kafka basics, delivery guarantees, idempotent consumers, dead-letter queues, backpressure and event-driven design, from mental model to production pitfalls.

chapters.title: Queues vs Pub/Sub Mental Model
points: Message queue: each message is consumed by exactly one consumer in a competing-consumers group (work distribution, e.g. SQS, RabbitMQ queue)
Pub/sub: each message is delivered to every subscriber (fan-out, e.g. SNS, Redis pub/sub, Kafka consumer groups each get a full copy)
Broker decouples producer and consumer in time, speed and failure: producer does not wait for the consumer
Queue deletes a message after ack; a log (Kafka) retains it by retention time/size so it can be replayed
Command vs event: a command says 'do X' to one handler; an event says 'X happened' to any number of listeners

chapters.title: Kafka Basics: Topics, Partitions, Offsets
points: Topic is split into partitions; each partition is an append-only ordered log, and ordering is guaranteed only within a partition
Message key is hashed to pick the partition, so the same key always lands in the same partition and keeps its order
Offset is a message's position in a partition; the consumer commits offsets to resume where it left off
Consumer group: each partition is read by exactly one consumer in the group, so max parallelism = number of partitions
Replication: each partition has a leader and followers; acks=all with min.insync.replicas=2 survives a broker loss without data loss

chapters.title: Delivery Guarantees and Idempotent Consumers
points: At-most-once: commit the offset before processing; a crash loses the message, nothing is duplicated
At-least-once: commit after processing; a crash causes redelivery, so duplicates are possible (the usual default)
Exactly-once is not free: Kafka gets it with idempotent producer (enable.idempotence=true) plus transactions, but only within Kafka; external side effects still need idempotency
Idempotent consumer: store a processed message ID (unique key or dedupe table) and skip repeats; make the dedupe check and the business write one transaction
Naturally idempotent operations: upsert or 'set status=paid' are safe to repeat, 'balance += 10' is not

chapters.title: Failures: Retries, Dead-Letter Queues and Backpressure
points: Retry transient errors with exponential backoff plus jitter and a max attempt cap; never retry in a tight loop
Dead-letter queue (DLQ): after N failed attempts, move the poison message aside so it stops blocking the queue (SQS maxReceiveCount)
A DLQ needs an alarm on its depth, the original payload plus error metadata, and a tested redrive path
Backpressure: when consumers lag behind producers, slow the producer, bound the queue and shed or buffer load instead of growing without limit
Watch consumer lag (latest offset minus committed offset) and queue age; scale consumers up to the partition count

chapters.title: Event-Driven Design Pitfalls
points: Event notification (small, 'order placed' plus ID) vs event-carried state transfer (full data, consumers need no callback)
Choreography (services react to events, loose coupling, hard to trace) vs orchestration (a central coordinator, explicit flow)
Dual-write bug: writing to the DB and publishing to the broker separately can lose one; fix with the transactional outbox pattern
Ordering is per key only: assuming global order, or a rebalance mid-processing, causes out-of-order handling
Version events and evolve schemas compatibly (add optional fields only), because old messages stay in the log and consumers upgrade at different times

chapters.title: Messaging Cheat Sheet
points: Queue = one consumer per message; pub/sub = every subscriber; Kafka = partitioned replayable log
Ordering only within a partition (same key); parallelism ≤ partition count
Default to at-least-once plus an idempotent consumer; commit offsets after processing
Retry with backoff and jitter, then DLQ with an alarm; monitor consumer lag
Use the outbox pattern for DB plus event atomicity; version your event schemas
